Seminar Title:

Rational Design of a ZIF-67/CuS Heterostructure for Efficient Visible-Light Photocatalysis toward Organophosphorus Pesticide Remediation and Ammonia Synthesis

Abstract:

The strategic development of multifunctional photocatalysts capable of simultaneously addressing environmental remediation and facilitating sustainable energy conversion continues to pose a significant challenge in materials research, largely due to the difficulty of achieving efficient charge separation while maintaining strong redox potentials across multiple catalytic pathways. In this study, a ZIF-67/CuS heterostructure responsive to visible light was prepared through a straightforward synthesis route, in which the close interfacial junction formed between p-type CuS and n-type ZIF-67 promotes cooperative charge transfer across the interface, minimizes electron-hole pair recombination, and strengthens the composite's overall photocatalytic activity. This optimized hybrid material demonstrated a marked improvement in photocatalytic efficiency, breaking down roughly 86.8% of the malathion within one hour under visible-light exposure, substantially exceeding the capabilities of pristine CuS and ZIF-67 materials. The breakdown process followed a pseudo-first-order kinetics. Scavenger-based radical trapping tests helped to clarify the reaction mechanism further, showing that hydroxyl radicals (&bullOH), superoxide radicals (&bullO₂⁻), and photogenerated holes (h⁺) act as the dominant reactive species responsible for degradation, which in turn confirms that charge carriers separate efficiently and migrate directionally across the ZIF-67/CuS junction. In addition to its pollutant-degrading ability, this composite proved to be highly versatile, showing notable performance in photocatalytic nitrogen fixation a reaction with strong relevance to environmentally friendly ammonia production under mild conditions. When exposed to UV-visible light, the material generated ammonia at a rate near 294 &mumolg⁻&sup1h-1, underscoring its promise as an eco-friendly substitute for energy-demanding traditional ammonia synthesis. Taken together, the composite's strong dual functionality spanning both environmental cleanup and energy applications can be attributed to the formation of an effective Z-scheme heterojunction, which retains the individual redox strengths of each semiconductor while driving spatially separated charge migration, ultimately boosting the supply of reactive species available for multiple photocatalytic functions
